profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a market surveillance software company after a pilot deployment of a new spoofing-detection model based on multilevel limit order book representations triggered a sharp rise in compliance analyst complaints. Over the past three trading days, the alert queue for NASDAQ small-cap symbols has nearly doubled, but analyst-confirmed manipulation cases have not increased. The team needs to diagnose whether the issue comes from the new cascaded contrastive representation pipeline, from data handling in production, or from how alerts are being grouped and reviewed. The agenda is to review the symptom, compare what changed between the pre-production evaluation and live rollout, identify the most likely root cause, and agree on a near-term fix to stabilize analyst workload before the next market open. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting decision: what to patch immediately, what to verify after the meeting, and what evidence will count as the issue being fixed.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: surveillance workflows, compliance operations, alert triage metrics, pilot rollouts
members.background: Elena previously worked in brokerage compliance operations and now manages the firm's surveillance product for exchange and broker-dealer clients; she is fluent in analyst review processes and client escalation patterns but does not work directly on model training code.
members.private_state: Elena wants to reduce analyst frustration quickly and avoid having the pilot client blame the new model release; she is willing to accept a temporary narrowing of alert coverage if the queue becomes manageable by tomorrow morning.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the model's 'precision dropped,' they are talking about analyst-confirmed useful alerts at the case level after alert consolidation, not raw event-level labels.
A 'duplicate alert' means multiple alerts tied to the same symbol-side episode within a short review window, because that is how analysts experience workload.
Rolling back or patching 'the detector' includes thresholding, alert grouping, and analyst-facing suppression rules around the score, not just the representation model itself.
The pilot's production setup is materially the same as the one used in final validation except for live market flow, because deployment prerequisites were already signed off last week.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: LOB feature pipelines, representation learning, supervised contrastive training, model serving
members.background: Ravi built the cascaded LOB representation module and productionized the spoofing classifier; he has a quantitative finance background and has spent the last two years working on sequence models for market abuse detection.
members.private_state: Ravi wants to protect confidence in the new representation pipeline and suspects the complaints are due to downstream alert handling rather than the model itself; he prefers a minimal, technically clean patch over any hurried rollback.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the model's 'precision dropped,' they mean event-level precision against labeled manipulation windows in the monitoring dataset, before any analyst consolidation logic.
A 'duplicate alert' means repeated emissions for the exact same scored event ID or overlapping inference window from the service, not semantically similar episodes grouped by analysts.
Fixing 'the detector' primarily means changing model-serving inputs, windowing, calibration, or the scoring service; case management and review bundling belong downstream and are separate systems.
The production market-data feed was switched to the same normalized 20-level book format used in offline validation, because the feed migration ticket was marked complete before launch.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether 'precision is down' after the rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means fewer analyst-useful cases per reviewed case bundle, judged after deduplication and case consolidation in the compliance workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means lower event-level positive predictive value against labeled manipulation windows in the model-monitoring dataset before workflow consolidation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In surveillance teams, 'precision' is common shorthand and both participants regularly use the same term confidently; because both are diagnosing the same complaints, each assumes the other is using the obvious operational definition from their own layer of the system.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree there are 'too many duplicates' in the queue.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means analysts are seeing several alerts for what they perceive as one spoofing episode in the same symbol over roughly a 10-minute review window.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi means the service may be emitting multiple alerts for the same inference window or identical event payload due to replay or retry behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'duplicate alerts' sounds operationally obvious, and both have seen dashboards showing inflation in counts; neither expects that the other is anchoring the term to a different unit of analysis.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in fixing the detector
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss making a 'quick detector fix' before market open.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena assumes the fix can include threshold changes, bundling rules, cooldown suppression, and other presentation-layer controls that reduce analyst load without retraining.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi assumes the fix refers only to the model and scoring pipeline, such as input normalization, sequence windowing, or calibration, while downstream case bundling is outside the detector scope.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-functional meetings, 'detector' is often used loosely to refer to the end-to-end alerting behavior; because both are focused on immediate stabilization, the broad phrase feels shared even though their mental system boundaries differ.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to production using the 'same 20-level setup' as validation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena presupposes deployment sign-off means production is running the already-approved normalized top-20 bid/ask depth format used in pilot validation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ravi presupposes the same thing because the feed migration ticket was closed, but he specifically imagines the engineering-normalized 20-level depth snapshot aligned to every 200 ms inference step.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither thinks the feed format itself is an open question because both believe it was settled before launch; the apparent shared confidence prevents them from unpacking whether 'same 20-level setup' also includes timing alignment and normalization details.
